newsitem.title: USA: Florida tobacco suit unites varied cast.
newsitem.headline: Florida tobacco suit unites varied cast.

text.p: In the Broin secondhand-smoke suit set to go to trial Monday, husband-and-wife lawyers will take on a host of tobacco industry legal talent before a judge who began his career as a radio announcer.
Here are thumbnail sketches of key players in the $5 billion Norma Broin v. Philip Morris Cos. Inc., et al., the first class-action suit to go to trial against big tobacco.

- The lead plaintiff, American Airlines flight attendant Norma Broin, 42, is a political conservative and Mormon who has never smoked. She decided to take on the tobacco industry after contracting cancer, now in remission, that forced removal of part of her lung.

Broin, a mother of two who is married to a U.S. Marine, said she blames her disease on cigarette smoke inhaled on jetliners during the years before smoking was banned on most U.S. flights. She called the difficult decision to file the suit a moral one: "For me, this just boils down to what's right and what's wrong. It's not right to do something that costs people their lives," she said.

- Plaintiffs' attorneys Stanley and Susan Rosenblatt have cast themselves as David to the tobacco industry's Goliath, likening their cases against cigarette makers to a moral crusade. The Rosenblatts' small practice -- they work with three other lawyers -- was built on personal-injury cases before Norma Broin came into their lives six years ago. They have financed the case to date out of their own pockets to the tune of some $500,000.

The Rosenblatts describe themselves as the ideal legal tag team, with Stanley, 60, the pugnacious litigator and Susan, 46, the patient scholar, writer and researcher. Orthodox Jews who have nine children, the couple does not work on Saturdays.
The Rosenblatts also represent plaintiffs in Engle v. R.J. Reynolds, seeking damages on behalf of 400,000 to 500,000 Florida cigarette smokers.

- The tobacco attorneys who have participated in pre-trial hearings have not said who will serve as lead defense counsel. Hugh Whiting, an attorney for R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. who has played a major role in pre-trial hearings, said Friday that the defense would not comment before trial.

Besides Whiting, a partner at Jones, Day, Reavis & Pogue in Cleveland, the most vocal industry attorneys in the pre-trial phase of the suit have included David Hardy, a partner at Shook, Hardy & Bacon of Kansas City, co-counsel for Lorillard Inc. and Philip Morris; and Edward Moss, senior partner at Miami's Anderson Moss Sherouse & Petros, co-counsel for Brown & Williamson Tobacco Co.

No matter who emerges as lead counsel -- the defense has hinted it will have about four major speakers -- they are certain to be amply represented. At a recent pre-trial hearing, Judge Robert Kaye asked how many tobacco lawyers would be present at trial. "About 200," one said, smiling.

- Circuit Judge Robert Kaye, 68, began his career as a radio announcer, but got his draft notice the same day he got what he called his "big break," the offer of an announcing job at NBC. He attended the University of Miami Law School under the GI bill, graduating in 1957 with a Juris Doctor degree but not practicing law for 13 years, instead continuing his radio career at several local radio stations.

He went to work for State Attorney Richard Gerstein in 1970, working his way up to chief of the Major Crimes Division in the state attorney's office over 12 years. Gov. Bob Graham, now a U.S. senator from Florida, appointed Kaye to a circuit judgeship in 1981.

The highest profile case over which Kaye presided, prior to Broin, was a libel suit brought by Southern Airways against Miami ABC affiliate WPLG-TV (Channel 10), which had done an investigation claiming the airline was a CIA front and had transported drugs from Colombia in its planes.
The jury ruled in favor of the television station.
